advisor.summary: Section 132(e) excludes from employee income any property or service whose value is so small and provision so infrequent that accounting for it is administratively impracticable — occasional snacks, group meals, modest holiday gifts of property, flowers for life events. Classified correctly, these stay deductible to the employer, tax-free to the employee, and entirely off payroll. The two hard edges do all the damage in practice: cash and gift cards are never de minimis at any amount, and frequency is half the test, so a routine perk becomes wages. Employer-provided phones ride their own safe harbor under Notice 2011-72. The 2026 wrinkle is deduction-side: §274(o) makes employer eating-facility and convenience-of-the-employer meal costs nondeductible for amounts paid after 2025, so on-site meal programs keep the employee exclusion but lose the write-off.
mechanics: The test of §132(e)(1) weighs value and frequency together: a small item provided occasionally is excludable, while the identical item provided routinely fails because frequency makes accounting practicable — and there is no statutory dollar line to hide behind.

Reg. §1.132-6(c) makes cash and cash equivalents — gift cards and general-purpose certificates — taxable wages regardless of amount; the narrow exception is occasional meal money or cab fare for overtime work, and 'occasional' carries all the weight.

Employer-provided cell phones have a separate safe harbor: under Notice 2011-72, a phone provided for noncompensatory business reasons is a working-condition fringe and its personal use is de minimis, with no logging required.

The regulations' own examples calibrate the category — occasional parties and picnics, holiday gifts of low-value property, coffee and doughnuts, occasional supper money: small, irregular, and impractical to track.

For amounts paid after December 31, 2025, §274(o) denies the employer deduction for eating-facility and §119 convenience meals; the §132(e) employee-side exclusion survives, but the employer economics of on-site meal programs changed.

Operative rules and examples; subsection (c) is the absolute no-cash, no-gift-card rule.
The employer cell-phone safe harbor: business-reason phones excludable, personal use de minimis, no records required.

requirements: Benefits that are genuinely small and genuinely occasional — frequency is half the test.
A written policy listing the perks provided and stating the no-cash, no-gift-card rule.
Payroll coordination: anything cash-like goes on the W-2; qualifying items stay off entirely.
For phones: a documented noncompensatory business reason — one memo covers the program.
risks: Gift cards are the universal exam finding: they are wages at any amount, and a payroll audit reclassifies them across every employee and every open year with back taxes and penalties — the cost of the cleanup always exceeds the cost of the policy.
Frequency creep converts perks into compensation — daily meal money or a standing monthly gift fails even at trivial dollar values.
There is no safe-harbor dollar amount; an adviser promising a fixed figure is calibrating, not citing.
Perks flowing mainly to owners read as disguised distributions rather than fringe benefits.
On-site meal programs lose the employer deduction in 2026 under §274(o) — clients budgeting on the old treatment will overstate the write-off.
stateNotes: Conformity: states starting from federal AGI or federal taxable income conform to the §132(e) exclusion automatically — properly classified perks never enter the state base.
PTET interaction: perk costs are ordinary entity deductions that already reduce the base of any pass-through entity tax election; no separate PTET step exists.
Missouri: conforms through its federal starting point (RSMo §143.121) with no fringe-benefit addback.
reviewChecklist: Perk inventory completed and each item classified: de minimis, working-condition, taxable wage, or 2026 deduction-limited meals.
Written fringe policy adopted with the no-cash rule and frequency guardrails.
Gift-card practices ended or deliberately routed through payroll as bonuses.

client.teaser: The small perks you already give can stay off everyone's tax forms.
client.headline: Keep the small stuff tax-free — for you and your team
plainEnglish: The tax law has a common-sense rule. Perks too small to be worth tracking do not count as taxable pay. Coffee and snacks, an occasional team lunch, flowers for a new baby, a modest holiday gift — the business deducts them, the employee owes nothing, and nothing touches a W-2.

There are two tripwires. Cash and gift cards never qualify. A $20 gift card is taxable wages, no matter how festive. And 'occasional' is part of the deal — the same perk given routinely becomes taxable pay.
Most businesses stumble on one of these without knowing it. It surfaces during a payroll audit, multiplied across every employee and every year. A simple one-page policy prevents the whole problem.
client.analogy: It is like the express lane at the store. Genuinely small and occasional sails right through. Push a full cart into it and the whole load gets pulled aside.
benefits: Team perks that cost less than equivalent raises
Nothing added to W-2s and no payroll tax
Company phones handled cleanly with one memo
Protection from the gift-card mistake most businesses make
steps: WE review the perks you currently give and flag anything mislabeled.

YOU follow the policy — real items, given occasionally, never cards or cash.
WE check in each year to keep the program clean.
